parts.description: A shallow gray nonstick-coated metal frying pan with a rounded rim, riveted side bracket, and a black molded plastic handle with a hanging hole.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be a typical 26–28 cm nonstick skillet with a shallow aluminum pan body and a polymer handle. A realistic total length is about 0.45–0.50 m including handle, pan diameter about 0.27–0.29 m, rim height about 0.045–0.060 m, and wall/base thickness roughly 2–4 mm. Comparable nonstick aluminum pans of this size are commonly 0.75–1.15 kg; 0.95 kg is a reasonable rigid-body mass estimate including the aluminum body, steel/aluminum rivets/bracket, and plastic handle. The dominant structural/contact material is nonstick-coated aluminum: the pan bowl and outer bottom occupy most of the surface and mass, while the black handle is a secondary plastic component. A composite material density of about 2400 kg/m^3 is used to represent aluminum substrate with coating and minor polymer parts; if mass is computed from a closed convex volume instead of true shell volume, the explicit mass should override automatic density-derived mass because the pan is hollow and thin-walled. Friction is estimated lower than bare metal because of the nonstick/anodized coating, but not as low as ideal PTFE due to roughness, edge contact, and possible textured exterior: static friction about 0.35 and dynamic friction about 0.28 are suitable general-purpose values. Restitution is set to 0.25 because the object is a thin metal/plastic assembly that may ring but dissipates energy through deformation, coating, handle compliance, and multi-point contact. The pan is concave, so a single convex hull would incorrectly fill the bowl and prevent objects from contacting the interior. For Isaac Sim/PhysX rigid-body use, convex decomposition is the recommended default: several convex hulls can represent the bottom disk, side wall/rim, handle, bracket, and rivet bumps with good performance. If high-fidelity interior contact is required for small objects resting inside the pan, an SDF mesh can be considered, but convex decomposition is more robust and efficient for most dynamic rigid-body scenes. Contact offset is kept small at 0.002 m for a 25–50 cm object to avoid visible hovering while maintaining stable contact generation; rest offset is 0.0 m so the collision surface aligns with the visual mesh. CCD is enabled at the body level because the pan has thin rim/wall features and a long handle that may be moved quickly, though it can be disabled for slow tabletop-only scenes. Gravity is given in Isaac Sim's typical Z-up convention. No articulation properties are physically active because this is a single rigid object with fixed rivets and no joints.
